work.title: FIELD SCHOOL
work.subtitle: 观察与提问课程讲义
work.framework: course: Practice response / distinct native A4 document layout
work.scope: Fictional adult visual-observation course. Not botanical identification, field safety instruction, certification or evidence about real learners.

pages.title: A course in noticing carefully.
pages.lead: Learn to distinguish a visible detail from the explanation you attach to it. The garden scenes are prompts for adult discussion, not a real field class or a verified site.
pages.body: The learning objective is to write one observation, identify one assumption and ask one source-aware question. Completion is a personal practice record, not an accredited qualification.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Write an observation without naming a cause.

pages.title: Read the learning route.
pages.lead: The ten-page route moves from description to interpretation, comparison and reflection. Read the numbered headings in order or return to the exercise that addresses your current question.
pages.body: Pages 3–4 practise neutral description. Pages 5–6 separate interpretation and context. Pages 7–8 compare wording and rehearse feedback. Pages 9–10 collect a bounded response and a next question.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Mark the exercise you want to revisit.

pages.title: Describe before explaining.
pages.lead: Choose one visible object in the illustration. Describe its shape, colour and relative position using ordinary language rather than a story about why it is there.
pages.body: For example, a blue gate is a visible detail. Calling the gate welcoming is an interpretation. Both may be useful, but they answer different questions and should not be merged into one finding.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Write two sentences labelled detail and interpretation.

pages.title: Keep the frame in view.
pages.lead: The picture has an edge. Anything outside that edge is not supplied by the exercise. A path disappearing behind a wall does not establish a destination, distance or accessible route.
pages.body: Practise naming one missing piece of context beside each observation. The aim is not to make the illustration less engaging; it is to make the limits of your description readable.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Name information that the frame does not supply.

pages.title: Offer more than one interpretation.
pages.lead: An empty bench could suggest quiet, an unoccupied moment or simply an artistic choice. The exercise contains no attendance record or statement of local preference.
pages.body: Write two plausible readings without choosing a winner. A useful interpretation remains connected to a visible detail while admitting what would need a separate source.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Offer a second reading of the same detail.

pages.title: Ask a source-aware question.
pages.lead: Turn an interpretation into a question that could be clarified with appropriate evidence. Keep the request narrow enough that another reader understands what information is missing.
pages.body: Replace Is this a good garden? with What real context would help us understand how this place is used? The latter does not invent a result or assume that the fictional place actually exists.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Rewrite a broad judgement as a bounded question.

pages.title: Compare two descriptions.
pages.lead: Read a short neutral description beside a more interpretive one. Identify which words introduce an assumption about use, mood or intent.
pages.body: The comparison is between sentences, not between real places or learner ability. No score, ranking or claim about participant performance is supplied.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Underline one word that reaches beyond the picture.

pages.title: Practise generous feedback.
pages.lead: Respond to another invented description by naming what is clear and asking what remains uncertain. This is a writing exercise, not an assessment of a real person.
pages.body: Try the response I can locate the blue gate; I cannot tell which source supports the claimed mood. Specific feedback is easier to act on than a global judgement such as good or bad.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Write one acknowledgement and one clarification question.

pages.title: Collect a learning response.
pages.lead: Bring together one observation, one assumption, one missing source and one next question. Keep the response compact enough that a reader can check each part.
pages.body: This response sheet is evidence of what you wrote in the exercise, not evidence that the illustrated setting has been studied. Do not include personal information about other participants.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Complete the four-part response in your own words.

pages.title: Leave with a better question.
pages.lead: Review which distinction became clearer: description versus interpretation, absence versus zero, or an attractive story versus a supported claim.
pages.body: Keep an earlier sentence and a revised sentence if that helps your reflection. This template supplies no passing grade or certificate; the useful outcome is a more precise question.
pages.detail: Use this section to record a bounded response to the question below. Retain the distinction between the fictional example, your interpretation and any separate evidence a real use would require.
pages.question: Name one question you can now ask more clearly.
